name: Cabling and Interface Errors
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Pick the right copper or fiber link, bring interfaces up, and diagnose duplex, speed and cable faults from interface counters.

lesson.intro: Most network outages that are not configuration mistakes are physical: the wrong cable, a cable that is too long, a dirty or swapped fiber, or two ends that disagree about speed and duplex. This pack covers the media on the CCNA blueprint (copper, multimode and single-mode fiber, shared and point-to-point Ethernet) and how to find interface and cable problems from status codes and show interfaces counters.
objectives: Choose UTP category, fiber type and connector for a given speed and distance
Pick straight-through or crossover cabling and explain what auto-MDIX changes
Bring a router interface up and interpret status and protocol codes
Diagnose speed mismatches, duplex mismatches and cable faults from show interfaces output

sections.title: Copper UTP: pairs, categories and the 100 meter rule
sections.body:
An office is being wired. Every desk gets a wall jack, every jack runs back to a patch panel in the wiring closet, and a short patch cable connects the panel to a switch. Almost all of that is **unshielded twisted pair (UTP)** copper: four pairs of wires, each pair twisted around itself, ending in an 8-pin **RJ-45** connector. The twists matter. Noise that hits a twisted pair hits both wires almost equally and cancels out, which cuts electromagnetic interference (EMI) and **crosstalk** between neighboring pairs. Where the electrical noise is extreme, such as next to factory motors, shielded twisted pair (STP) or fiber is used instead.

IEEE Ethernet names tell you the speed and medium. In **1000BASE-T**, 1000 is the speed in Mbps, BASE means baseband signaling, and T means twisted-pair copper. Every common UTP Ethernet standard has the same limit: **100 meters** per link, from switch port to device, patch cords included. Go past it and the signal weakens (attenuation) until frames get corrupted.

The cable must be good enough for the speed. The categories you will meet:

- **Cat5e:** 1 Gbps up to 100 m. The practical minimum today.
- **Cat6:** 1 Gbps at 100 m, and 10 Gbps only up to about 55 m.
- **Cat6a:** 10 Gbps over the full 100 m. The usual choice for new installs and for multigigabit APs.
- **Cat8:** 25 or 40 Gbps over short runs (about 30 m), used inside data centers.
sections.code:
Standard      IEEE       Speed      Medium                       Max length
10BASE-T      802.3i     10 Mbps    UTP, Cat3 or better          100 m
100BASE-TX    802.3u     100 Mbps   UTP, Cat5 or better          100 m
1000BASE-T    802.3ab    1 Gbps     UTP, Cat5e or better         100 m
10GBASE-T     802.3an    10 Gbps    UTP, Cat6a (Cat6 to ~55 m)   100 m
1000BASE-SX   802.3z     1 Gbps     multimode fiber              about 550 m
1000BASE-LX   802.3z     1 Gbps     single-mode fiber            5 km (more with LX/LH optics)
10GBASE-SR    802.3ae    10 Gbps    multimode fiber              300 to 400 m
10GBASE-LR    802.3ae    10 Gbps    single-mode fiber            10 km
sections.pitfall: Forgetting the patch cords. The 100 meter budget covers the whole channel: patch cord, wall run and the cord at the desk. A 95 meter wall run plus two long patch cables is already over.

check.question: A new wall jack is 120 meters of cable away from the nearest switch. What is the problem with running 1000BASE-T to it?
choices: It must use a crossover cable at that length
It exceeds the 100 meter UTP limit, so expect errors or no link
Only Cat3 cable can carry 1000BASE-T that far
check.explanation: UTP Ethernet standards, including 1000BASE-T, allow 100 meters per link. At 120 meters attenuation corrupts frames or prevents the link from coming up. Fix it with a closer switch or a fiber uplink.

sections.title: Straight-through, crossover and auto-MDIX
sections.body:
Plug a PC into a switch and it works. Plug two old switches together with the same kind of cable and the link stays dark. The reason is which pins each device transmits on. For 10BASE-T and 100BASE-TX, only two pairs are used:

- PCs, servers, routers and APs **transmit on pins 1 and 2** and receive on pins 3 and 6.
- Switches and hubs do the opposite: they **transmit on pins 3 and 6** and receive on 1 and 2.

A **straight-through** cable connects pin 1 to pin 1, 2 to 2, and so on. That works between unlike devices, because one side's transmit pins land on the other side's receive pins. When both ends transmit on the same pins, you need a **crossover** cable, which connects 1,2 on one end to 3,6 on the other. The rule:

- Devices from different groups (PC to switch, router to switch, AP to switch): **straight-through**.
- Devices from the same group (switch to switch, router to router, PC to PC, PC directly to router): **crossover**.

1000BASE-T uses all four pairs and transmits and receives on each pair at the same time, but the same idea holds: a gigabit crossover cable also swaps the pair on pins 4,5 with the pair on pins 7,8.

In real life you rarely think about this, because of **auto-MDIX**. A port with auto-MDIX notices that it is receiving on its own transmit pins and swaps them internally, so either cable type works. Cisco switches enable it by default (`mdix auto`), and it generally needs speed and duplex left on auto. The exam still expects you to pick the correct cable for a drawing, as if auto-MDIX were not there.
sections.code:
Transmit on pins 1,2  (like a PC)     Transmit on pins 3,6  (like a switch)
---------------------------------     -------------------------------------
PC and server NICs                    LAN switches
Routers                               Hubs
Access points (Ethernet port)

Same column    -> crossover cable      (switch-switch, router-router, PC-router)
Different      -> straight-through     (PC-switch, router-switch, AP-switch)

Straight-through           Crossover (10/100 pairs)
 end A    end B             end A    end B
   1 ------ 1                 1 ------ 3
   2 ------ 2                 2 ------ 6
   3 ------ 3                 3 ------ 1
   6 ------ 6                 6 ------ 2
sections.tip: The console cable (a rollover or USB console cable) connects a laptop to a device's console port for management. It is never used for Ethernet data links.
sections.pitfall: Assuming "router to PC" is straight-through because they look like different devices. On the pin chart they are the same kind of device, so the exam answer is crossover.

check.question: Without auto-MDIX, which cable connects a PC directly to a router's Ethernet port?
choices: Straight-through, because they are different kinds of device
Crossover, because both transmit on pins 1 and 2
Rollover, because the router needs a console
Either one, because routers always swap pins
check.explanation: PCs and routers are in the same group: both transmit on pins 1 and 2. Same group means crossover. The rollover cable is for the console port, not for Ethernet.

sections.title: Fiber: multimode, single-mode, connectors and optics
sections.body:
Two buildings in an office park are 400 meters apart, and the company also links to a data center 12 km away. Copper cannot reach either one. **Fiber-optic** cable sends light through a glass **core**. The surrounding **cladding** reflects the light back into the core, and outer layers protect the glass. Light has no electrical noise problems, so fiber is immune to EMI, and it does not leak signals that someone could tap, which also makes it more secure.

There are two kinds, and the difference is the size of the core:

- **Multimode fiber (MMF)** has a wide core (50 or 62.5 microns). Light enters at many angles (modes), and those paths have slightly different lengths, so pulses smear out over distance (modal dispersion). Cheaper optics using LEDs or VCSEL lasers. Reach: hundreds of meters, for example within a building or between nearby buildings.
- **Single-mode fiber (SMF)** has a tiny core (about 9 microns). A laser sends light along essentially one path, so it travels kilometers to tens of kilometers. The optics cost more.

Every fiber link uses two strands, one per direction, with the transmitter at one end connected to the receiver at the other. Switches take fiber through pluggable transceivers: **SFP** (1 Gbps), **SFP+** (10 Gbps), **QSFP+** and **QSFP28** (40 and 100 Gbps). The optic, the fiber type and the far-end optic must all match: a 10GBASE-SR optic talks to another SR optic over multimode, a 10GBASE-LR optic talks to another LR over single-mode.

Connectors to recognize: **LC** (small, with a latch, the standard on SFP and SFP+ modules), **SC** (larger square push-pull), **ST** (round bayonet twist-lock, mostly older multimode installs) and **MPO** (many fibers in one connector, for 40 and 100 Gbps parallel optics).
sections.code:
UTP copper        Multimode fiber      Single-mode fiber
Typical max length   100 m             ~300 to 550 m        5 to 40+ km
Core / medium        copper pairs      50 or 62.5 micron    ~9 micron
Light source         (electrical)      LED or VCSEL         laser
Cost of cable        low               medium               medium
Cost of optics/port  low               medium               high
EMI sensitivity      some              none                 none
Signal emissions     some              none                 none
sections.pitfall: Swapping the two strands so transmit meets transmit. Each end then sends light into the other end's transmitter, no light reaches either receiver, and the link stays down/down. Roll the strands at one end.

check.question: Two campus buildings are 8 km apart. Which medium fits the link?
check.explanation: Only single-mode fiber reaches kilometers: 10GBASE-LR, for example, runs 10 km. Multimode reaches hundreds of meters and UTP 100 meters at most (Cat8 only about 30 meters).

sections.title: Shared media versus point-to-point Ethernet
sections.body:
Old Ethernet LANs used **hubs**. A hub is a Layer 1 device: it regenerates every electrical signal it receives and repeats it out every other port. It never reads a MAC address. If two PCs on a hub transmit at the same moment, their signals collide and both frames are destroyed. All the devices on a hub share the bandwidth and form one **collision domain**, which is what the blueprint calls **Ethernet shared media**.

To share, devices on a hub run **half duplex** with **CSMA/CD** (carrier sense multiple access with collision detection):

1. Listen until nobody else is sending.
2. Start sending the frame.
3. Keep listening while sending, to detect a collision.
4. On a collision, send a jam signal so everyone knows.
5. Wait a random backoff time, then start again.

Switches changed everything. Each switch port connects to exactly one device, so each cable is a **point-to-point** link with only two devices on it. With a separate transmit and receive path and nobody else on the wire, both ends can send at the same time: **full duplex**. CSMA/CD is turned off, collisions cannot happen, and every link carries traffic independently of the others. Each switch port is still called its own collision domain, even though a full-duplex link never sees a collision.

That gives you a powerful troubleshooting rule: on a modern full-duplex link, the collision counters should stay at zero. Collisions on a switch port mean either a hub or half-duplex device is attached, or something is misconfigured.
sections.code:
Shared media (hub)                     Point-to-point (switch)

PC1   PC2   PC3   PC4                  PC1   PC2   PC3   PC4
  \    |     |    /                     |     |     |     |
   +--[  HUB  ]--+                     +-[    SWITCH    ]-+
one collision domain, half duplex,     four links, four collision domains,
everyone shares the bandwidth          full duplex, no collisions
sections.pitfall: Reading any collision counter as a fault. On a half-duplex link some collisions are normal CSMA/CD behavior. Collisions on a link that should be full duplex, and late collisions anywhere, are the warning signs.

check.question: Four PCs connect to a hub, and the hub connects to a switch port. Which statement is true?
choices: Each PC has its own collision domain
The hub forwards frames only to the destination MAC address
The PCs can all run full duplex
The four PCs and the switch port share one collision domain and must use half duplex
check.explanation: A hub repeats every signal everywhere, so everything attached to it, including the switch port, is one collision domain. Those devices must use half duplex and CSMA/CD. Full duplex and per-port collision domains need a switch.

sections.title: Bringing an interface up and reading its status
sections.body:
A brand-new router arrives. You cable its GigabitEthernet0/0 to the office switch, but nothing works. That is expected: **router interfaces start administratively down** (shut down) until you enable them. **Switch ports start enabled**, which is why a switch works out of the box. Bringing a router LAN interface up takes three things: an address, a mask and `no shutdown`.

The fastest way to check every interface is `show ip interface brief`. Read the last two columns together. **Status** (also called line status) is mostly about Layer 1: is there a working physical connection? **Protocol** is about Layer 2: is the data link working?

- **administratively down / down:** the interface has `shutdown` configured. Fix: `no shutdown`.
- **down / down:** Layer 1 problem: no cable, bad cable, wrong cable type, speed mismatch, or the far end is off or shut down.
- **up / down:** Layer 1 is fine but Layer 2 is not, for example mismatched encapsulation or keepalives on a serial WAN link. Not expected on LAN switch ports.
- **up / up:** working.

On switches, `show interfaces status` gives the same information as one word: **connected** (up/up), **notconnect** (down/down), **disabled** (administratively down) and **err-disabled** (a feature such as port security shut the port for you; fix the cause, then `shutdown` and `no shutdown`).
sections.code:
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description LAN to office switch SW1
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/0, changed state to up
%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/0, changed state to up
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     192.168.1.1     YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
sections.tip: Read show ip interface brief right to left: protocol down with status up points at Layer 2; both down points at Layer 1 or a shutdown.
sections.pitfall: Typing ip address in global configuration mode. IP addresses belong to an interface, so enter interface configuration mode first (the prompt changes to config-if).

activity.title: Bring up a router LAN interface
activity.prompt: Run show ip interface brief first and note the "administratively down" state on every port. Then name the router R1, give G0/0 the address 192.168.1.1/24 and enable it. Run show ip interface brief again and compare the Status and Protocol columns before and after.

check.question: show ip interface brief lists G0/1 as "administratively down    down". What fixes it?
choices: Change the duplex setting to full
check.explanation: "Administratively down" means someone (or the factory default on a router) configured shutdown. The interface command no shutdown enables it. A cable problem would show down/down instead.

sections.title: Speed, duplex and autonegotiation
sections.body:
A user complains the link to a file server is "up but painfully slow, and worse when it is busy". Both ends show the link up. This is the classic **duplex mismatch**, and to understand it you need autonegotiation.

10/100/1000 Ethernet ports use IEEE **autonegotiation** by default. Both ends advertise what they support and pick the fastest speed and best duplex they share. When both sides negotiate, it just works. The trouble starts when one side is hard-coded. On Cisco switches, configuring both `speed` and `duplex` disables autonegotiation on that port. The other end keeps trying, gets no answer, and falls back to defaults:

- **Speed:** it can sense the speed from the electrical signal, so it usually gets speed right.
- **Duplex:** it cannot sense duplex, so it uses the IEEE default: **half duplex at 10 or 100 Mbps, full duplex at 1000 Mbps**.

So if SW2 is hard-coded `speed 100` and `duplex full`, and SW1 is on auto, SW1 senses 100 Mbps and picks half duplex. Now SW2 sends whenever it likes (full duplex) while SW1 follows CSMA/CD rules, thinks it sees collisions, and aborts its own frames. The link is up/up, so nothing looks broken at a glance, but throughput collapses under load. SW1, the half-duplex side, counts **collisions and late collisions**. SW2, the full-duplex side, receives the chopped-off frames as **runts and CRC errors**.

A **speed mismatch** is different and easier: two ends hard-coded to different speeds cannot understand each other at all, so the link stays down/down (notconnect).

The fix for both is the same principle: set both ends to auto, or hard-code both ends to the same speed and duplex. `show interfaces status` helps here, because it prefixes negotiated values with **a-**. In `a-full a-100` the switch negotiated; in `full 100` someone configured it.
sections.code:
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# speed 100
SW2(config-if)# duplex full

SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 status
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/1                        connected    trunk      a-half  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX

! a- means autonegotiated. SW1 had to fall back to its default: half duplex at 100 Mbps.
sections.pitfall: Expecting a duplex mismatch to bring the link down. It does not: the link is up/up and passes some traffic, which is exactly why it is hard to spot. Compare the duplex on both ends.

check.question: SW2's port is hard-coded to speed 100 and duplex full. SW1's connected port is left on auto. What does SW1 end up using?
check.explanation: SW2 no longer sends autonegotiation messages, so SW1 senses the speed (100) and uses the IEEE default duplex for that speed, which is half. The result is a duplex mismatch: SW1 half, SW2 full.

sections.title: Reading show interfaces counters
sections.body:
When a link is up but misbehaving, `show interfaces` holds the evidence. Every frame that fails a check is counted. The counters you must be able to read:

- **Runts:** frames smaller than the 64-byte Ethernet minimum. Usually the debris of collisions or a duplex mismatch.
- **Giants:** frames larger than the maximum (1518 bytes for a standard frame). Often an MTU mismatch, such as one side sending jumbo frames, or a faulty NIC.
- **CRC:** frames whose frame check sequence (FCS) did not match, so bits changed in transit. Damaged cable, bad connector, EMI, or the full-duplex side of a duplex mismatch.
- **Input errors:** a total that includes runts, giants, CRC, frame, overrun and ignored counts.
- **Collisions:** normal in moderation on half duplex, never expected on full duplex.
- **Late collisions:** collisions detected after the first 64 bytes were sent. In a correctly cabled LAN that cannot happen, so late collisions point to a duplex mismatch (or a cable far beyond spec).
- **Output errors and interface resets:** trouble sending, often from the same physical causes.

Two habits make you good at this. First, a counter is history: 40 CRC errors from last month mean nothing. Run `clear counters`, wait, and look again to see what is **incrementing now**. Second, read counters together: CRC errors with no collisions on a full-duplex port point at the cable; late collisions on a half-duplex port point at duplex.
sections.code:
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1
GigabitEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is up (connected)
  Hardware is Gigabit Ethernet, address is 0019.e86a.6f81 (bia 0019.e86a.6f81)
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 100000 Kbit/sec, DLY 100 usec,
  Half-duplex, 100Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
  ! lines omitted
     2295197 packets input, 305539992 bytes, 0 no buffer
     0 runts, 0 giants, 0 throttles
     0 input errors, 0 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
     3594664 packets output, 436549843 bytes, 0 underruns
     0 output errors, 1793 collisions, 3 interface resets
     0 babbles, 1564 late collision, 0 deferred

Symptom                                        Likely cause                     Fix
down/down (notconnect)                         no or bad cable, wrong cable,    check cable and optics,
                                               speed mismatch, far end down     match speeds, no shutdown
CRC and input errors rising, no collisions     damaged cable, EMI, connector    replace or reroute the cable
Late collisions on a half-duplex port          duplex mismatch                  auto on both ends, or both full
Runts and CRC on the full-duplex neighbor      duplex mismatch                  same fix
Giants                                         MTU mismatch, faulty NIC         match MTU on both ends
sections.pitfall: Diagnosing from a single snapshot. Counters accumulate since the last reload or clear counters. Clear them, generate traffic, and check again before you replace hardware.

check.question: Which counter is the strongest single sign of a duplex mismatch on a half-duplex interface?
check.explanation: On a properly built LAN, collisions happen within the first 64 bytes. A full-duplex neighbor sends whenever it likes, so the half-duplex side sees collisions late in its frames. Giants point to MTU or NIC problems instead.

keyTerms.definition: Unshielded twisted pair: four twisted copper pairs with RJ-45 connectors, limited to 100 m per Ethernet link.
Cable that connects the transmit pins at one end to the receive pins at the other; needed between like devices without auto-MDIX.
Port feature that detects the cable type and swaps transmit and receive pairs internally, so either cable works.
Fiber with a wide 50 or 62.5 micron core; cheaper optics, reach of hundreds of meters.
Fiber with a roughly 9 micron core and laser optics; reaches kilometers to tens of kilometers.
Half-duplex Ethernet rules: listen, send, detect collisions, jam, back off a random time, retry.
One end half duplex, the other full. The link stays up but performs badly, with late collisions on the half side.
A received frame smaller than the 64-byte Ethernet minimum.
A received frame larger than the maximum allowed size, usually from an MTU mismatch.
A frame whose FCS check failed because bits changed in transit; usually a physical problem.
A collision detected after the first 64 bytes of a frame; points to a duplex mismatch.

summary: UTP Ethernet reaches 100 m per link; use Cat6a for 10GBASE-T at full length and fiber beyond 100 m.
Like devices need a crossover cable and unlike devices a straight-through, unless auto-MDIX fixes it for you.
Multimode fiber covers hundreds of meters with cheaper optics; single-mode covers kilometers with lasers; LC is the common SFP connector.
Router interfaces start shut down: administratively down needs no shutdown, down/down is Layer 1, up/down is Layer 2.
Speed mismatch keeps the link down; duplex mismatch keeps it up but slow, with late collisions on the half-duplex side and runts and CRC errors on the other.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a junior technician why a link can show up/up and still be terrible, using a duplex mismatch as the example, and say which counters prove it.

questions.question: What is the maximum length, in meters, of a 1000BASE-T link over UTP?
questions.explanation: Every common UTP Ethernet standard (10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX, 1000BASE-T and 10GBASE-T on Cat6a) allows 100 meters per link, including patch cords.

questions.question: A new AP supports 10 Gbps uplinks over copper and sits 90 meters from the switch. Which cable category supports 10GBASE-T at that length?
questions.explanation: Cat6a is rated for 10GBASE-T over the full 100 meters. Cat6 supports 10 Gbps only up to about 55 meters, and Cat5e is meant for 1 Gbps.

questions.question: Why are the wires in UTP cable twisted in pairs?
choices: So that noise affects both wires equally and cancels, reducing EMI and crosstalk
To make the cable easier to bend around corners
To let the cable carry light as well as electricity
To allow the cable to exceed 100 meters
questions.explanation: Twisting means outside interference and crosstalk induce nearly the same voltage on both wires of a pair, and the receiver cancels it out. It does not extend the distance limit or change what the cable carries.

questions.question: Which cable type connects a PC to a switch access port when auto-MDIX is not in play?
questions.explanation: The PC transmits on pins 1,2 and the switch on pins 3,6, so a straight-through cable lines transmit up with receive. Crossover is for like devices, and rollover is for console access.

questions.question: Auto-MDIX is disabled everywhere. Which two connections need a crossover cable? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Crossover cables join devices that transmit on the same pins. Two switches both transmit on 3,6; a router and a PC both transmit on 1,2. PC, router and AP to a switch are unlike pairs, so straight-through.

questions.question: On a 100BASE-TX link, which pins does a LAN switch port transmit on?
questions.explanation: Switches and hubs transmit on pins 3 and 6 and receive on 1 and 2, the opposite of PCs and routers. Pins 4,5 and 7,8 are unused by 10/100 Ethernet and only matter for 1000BASE-T.

questions.question: Two older switches without auto-MDIX are joined with a straight-through cable. Both ports are on auto speed and duplex. What will show interfaces status most likely show on both ends?
questions.explanation: Both switches transmit on pins 3,6, so with a straight-through cable each transmitter feeds the other's transmitter and no signal reaches either receiver. The link never comes up, which shows as notconnect (down/down).

questions.question: A company needs a 10 Gbps link to a data center 10 km away. Which medium should it use?
questions.explanation: 10GBASE-LR over single-mode fiber reaches 10 km. 10GBASE-SR over multimode stops at a few hundred meters, and copper stops at 100 meters or less.

questions.question: Why does multimode fiber support shorter distances than single-mode fiber?
choices: It uses electrical signals instead of light
Its wider core lets light take many paths of different lengths, which smears the pulses over distance
Its core is narrower, so less light gets through
It can only carry one direction of traffic
questions.explanation: Multimode's 50 or 62.5 micron core lets light bounce along many paths (modes). Pulses arrive spread out in time, which limits distance. Single-mode's tiny core keeps light on essentially one path.

questions.question: Which small, latching fiber connector is used on most SFP and SFP+ transceivers?
questions.explanation: LC is the small form factor connector that fits the duplex ports on SFP and SFP+ modules. SC is a larger square connector, ST is an older bayonet type, and RJ-45 is for copper.

questions.question: Match each Ethernet standard to its medium and reach.
questions.explanation: T means twisted-pair copper. In the fiber names, S means short-wavelength optics for multimode and L means long-wavelength optics for single-mode.

questions.question: After a fiber patch panel was rearranged, a 10GBASE-LR link between two switches shows down/down at both ends. Both optics are 10GBASE-LR and the fiber is single-mode. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A duplex mismatch between the optics
The link exceeds the 100 meter limit
The transmit and receive strands are swapped, so transmit meets transmit
questions.explanation: Each fiber link needs transmit at one end connected to receive at the other. If the strands are crossed wrongly, no light reaches either receiver and the link stays down. Fiber ignores EMI, fiber links do not have a duplex mismatch problem, and the 100 meter limit applies to UTP.

questions.question: What does a hub do with an incoming frame?
choices: Forwards it only out the port where the destination MAC address was learned
Repeats the electrical signal out every other port
Routes it based on the destination IP address
Drops it unless it is a broadcast
questions.explanation: A hub is a Layer 1 multiport repeater. It does not understand frames or addresses; it just regenerates the signal out all other ports, which is why devices on a hub share one collision domain.

questions.question: Put the CSMA/CD steps a half-duplex Ethernet device follows in order.
items: Listen until no other device is sending
Keep listening while sending to detect a collision
If a collision occurs, send a jam signal
Wait a random backoff time, then try again
questions.explanation: Carrier sense (listen), multiple access (anyone may send), collision detection (listen while sending), then jam and a random backoff so the colliding devices do not collide again immediately.

questions.question: Which statement describes point-to-point Ethernet links in a switched LAN?
choices: All links share one collision domain, so only one device can send at a time
Each link must run half duplex because switches use CSMA/CD
Each link connects two devices that can run full duplex, so collisions cannot occur
Links only work if a hub is placed between the switches
questions.explanation: A switch port connects to exactly one device, so with separate send and receive paths both can transmit at once. Full duplex disables CSMA/CD and collisions cannot happen.

questions.question: You are in interface configuration mode on a router port that shows "administratively down". Which command enables it?
questions.explanation: Router interfaces are shut down by default. no shutdown enables the interface; shutdown disables it again.

questions.question: Which privileged EXEC command lists every interface with its IP address, status and protocol in one line each?
questions.explanation: show ip interface brief gives one line per interface with the IP address, the method used to set it, the status (Layer 1) and the protocol (Layer 2). It is usually the first command in any interface check.

questions.question: Put the commands to give a new router's G0/0 the address 192.168.1.1/24 and bring it up in order, starting from user EXEC mode.
questions.explanation: Move from user EXEC to privileged EXEC, then global configuration, then interface configuration. The address and no shutdown are interface subcommands, so they come last.

questions.question: Match each interface state to its most likely cause.

pairs.right: No cable, bad cable or the far end is off
Layer 2 problem such as an encapsulation mismatch
A feature such as port security shut the port

questions.explanation: Status reflects Layer 1 and protocol reflects Layer 2. Administratively down is always the shutdown command, while err-disabled means the switch disabled the port itself because of an error condition.

questions.question: Based on the exhibit, which statement is correct?
questions.code:
R2# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     10.1.1.1        YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     10.1.2.1        YES manual administratively down down
GigabitEthernet0/2     10.1.3.1        YES manual down                  down
choices: G0/1 is shut down and needs no shutdown
G0/0 has a physical problem such as a bad cable
G0/2 has an IP address problem
G0/1 has a speed mismatch with its neighbor
questions.explanation: G0/1 shows administratively down, which only happens when shutdown is configured. G0/0 is up/up and working. G0/2 is down/down, which points to a Layer 1 issue on G0/2, not on G0/1.

questions.question: In the exhibit, which port was most likely shut down by the switch itself because of a port security violation?
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces status
Port      Name          Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/1     Uplink-D1     connected    trunk      a-full  a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/2     Spare         disabled     1          auto    auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/3     Room-204      notconnect   10         auto    auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/4     Lobby-kiosk   err-disabled 10         auto    auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
questions.explanation: err-disabled means the switch disabled the port because of an error condition, and a port security violation is the classic cause. disabled (Gi0/2) means an administrator configured shutdown, and notconnect (Gi0/3) is a Layer 1 problem.

questions.question: One end of a link is hard-coded to 100 Mbps and the other to 1000 Mbps. What happens?
choices: The link stays down (notconnect) because the two ends cannot agree on signaling
The link comes up at 100 Mbps with a duplex mismatch
The link comes up at 1000 Mbps
The link comes up but drops every broadcast
questions.explanation: Two ends hard-coded to different speeds cannot decode each other at all, so the link stays down/down. A duplex mismatch, in contrast, leaves the link up.

questions.question: Which interface subcommand forces a switch port to full duplex?
questions.explanation: duplex full sets the duplex manually. On Cisco switches, setting both speed and duplex disables autonegotiation on the port, so configure the other end to match.

questions.question: SW1 shows the output in the exhibit for the link to SW2. What is the best interpretation?
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 status
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/1     Link-to-SW2        connected    trunk      a-half  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX
choices: Both switches negotiated 100 Mbps half duplex successfully
SW1 was manually configured to half duplex
The link has a speed mismatch and is down
SW1 autonegotiated but SW2 likely has autonegotiation disabled, probably hard-coded to full duplex
questions.explanation: The a- prefix means SW1 autonegotiated. Two negotiating gigabit ports would pick a-full a-1000. Falling back to half at 100 means SW1 heard no negotiation and used defaults, so SW2 is hard-coded, almost certainly to 100/full: a duplex mismatch.

questions.question: Which two practices prevent a duplex mismatch on a switch-to-switch link? (Choose two.)
choices: Hard-code full duplex on one end and leave the other on auto
Hard-code the same speed and duplex on both ends
Hard-code only the end with the faster port
questions.explanation: Mismatches come from one end negotiating while the other does not. Either let both negotiate or configure both identically. Auto-MDIX is about cable pinouts, not duplex.

questions.question: Which symptom is typical of a duplex mismatch?
choices: The link is up/up but slow, with errors that grow under load
questions.explanation: A duplex mismatch does not stop the link from coming up. The half-duplex side backs off and aborts frames, so performance gets worse as traffic increases.

questions.question: What is a runt?
choices: A frame smaller than the 64-byte Ethernet minimum
A frame with a valid FCS but no data
A frame that arrived after the aging timer expired
questions.explanation: Runts are undersized frames, below 64 bytes. They are usually fragments left over from collisions or a duplex mismatch. Oversized frames are giants.

questions.question: What is the minimum valid Ethernet frame size in bytes (destination MAC through FCS)?
questions.explanation: An Ethernet frame must be at least 64 bytes from the destination MAC address through the FCS; the sender pads short data. Anything smaller is counted as a runt. The standard maximum is 1518 bytes.

questions.question: The counters in the exhibit keep increasing between two outputs taken a minute apart. What is the most likely cause?
questions.code:
SW3# show interfaces gigabitethernet1/0/12
GigabitEthernet1/0/12 is up, line protocol is up (connected)
  Hardware is Gigabit Ethernet, address is 7c95.f3a1.200c (bia 7c95.f3a1.200c)
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,
  Full-duplex, 1000Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
  ! lines omitted
     8817243 packets input, 1100315532 bytes, 0 no buffer
     0 runts, 0 giants, 0 throttles
     4318 input errors, 4318 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
     9120034 packets output, 2104879551 bytes, 0 underruns
     0 output errors, 0 collisions, 0 interface resets
     0 babbles, 0 late collision, 0 deferred
choices: A duplex mismatch with the connected device
An MTU mismatch causing oversized frames
A damaged cable, bad connector or electrical interference
The port is in the wrong VLAN
questions.explanation: CRC errors are climbing on a full-duplex gigabit port with zero collisions and zero runts or giants. That pattern means bits are being corrupted on the wire: a physical cable, connector or EMI problem. A duplex mismatch would also show collisions or runts.

questions.question: SW1 was configured to send jumbo frames of 9000 bytes on its uplink. Its neighbor SW2 still uses the standard 1500-byte MTU. Which counter will grow on SW2's interface?
questions.explanation: Frames above the maximum size that the receiving port accepts are counted as giants. An MTU mismatch like this is the most common cause. Collisions and late collisions involve duplex, and runts are undersized frames.

questions.question: Match each show interfaces counter to what it means.

pairs.right: Frames longer than the maximum size
Frames that failed the FCS check
Collision after the first 64 bytes were sent
Total of runts, giants, CRC and other receive errors

questions.explanation: Input errors is the umbrella counter. CRC means corrupted bits, runts and giants are size problems, and late collisions are the signature of a duplex mismatch.

questions.question: Before re-checking a link for new errors, you want to reset all interface counters to zero. Which privileged EXEC command does that?
questions.explanation: clear counters resets the show interfaces counters (IOS asks you to confirm). Then you can see which errors are still incrementing instead of reading old history.

questions.question: Based on the exhibit, what is the most likely problem on this link?

  Hardware is Gigabit Ethernet, address is 7c95.f3a1.2007 (bia 7c95.f3a1.2007)
  Half-duplex, 100Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX

choices: A damaged cable causing CRC errors
Nothing; collisions are normal on gigabit links
A duplex mismatch, with this port running half duplex
questions.explanation: The port runs half duplex at 100 Mb/s on a gigabit-capable interface and shows many late collisions with no CRC errors. That is the half-duplex side of a duplex mismatch, likely because the neighbor is hard-coded to full duplex.
